Gravitation from Hilbert-Space Granularity:
The Sphere, the String, and the Ring

Andrew Korytko ORCID andrew@alphalatitude.com

AlphaLatitude Inc., P.O. Box 64341, Sunnyvale, California 94088, USA

Abstract

In Palmer’s Rational Quantum Mechanics, Hilbert space is granular, with a parameter LLL that he attributes to gravity. We reverse the order: LLL comes first, one universal integer, and two postulates place his bit strings on rings of at most LLL cells. The postulates give L2/4−L/2+1L^2/4 - L/2 + 1L2/4−L/2+1 largest rings, and thermodynamics gives an observer’s cosmological horizon one bit of entropy for each. Jacobson’s thermodynamic argument gives Einstein’s equations, in which the length of a cell sets Newton’s constant and the length of a largest ring the cosmological constant. The measured GGG and Λ\LambdaΛ fix the cell at πln⁡2\sqrt{\pi\ln2}πln2​ Planck lengths and LLL at 4.4×10614.4\times10^{61}4.4×1061, to leading order in 1/L1/L1/L. A body’s energy is held by the strings that carry its information, and the strings’ energies, spread at the horizon’s temperature, average one thermal energy of the horizon. With equipartition and maximum entropy, these give the radial acceleration relation of galaxies, a function previously fitted to the data, with its scale a0=(1−ln⁡2)c2/2ln⁡2 RΛ=1.200×10−10a_0 = (1-\ln2)c^2/2\ln2\,\RL = 1.200\times10^{-10}a0​=(1−ln2)c2/2ln2RΛ​=1.200×10−10 m s−2^{-2}−2, RΛ\RLRΛ​ the horizon radius, where (1.20±0.24)(1.20\pm0.24)(1.20±0.24) and (1.19±0.10)×10−10(1.19\pm0.10)\times10^{-10}(1.19±0.10)×10−10 m s−2^{-2}−2 are measured. The strings hold all the energy inside the horizon, and the vacuum’s part of it, their heat, is the share ΩΛ=ln⁡2=0.693\Omega_\Lambda = \ln2 = 0.693ΩΛ​=ln2=0.693, where Planck measures 0.685±0.0070.685\pm0.0070.685±0.007. The integer LLL caps a random state, one in which every joint outcome of the other qubits occurs and leaves the last qubit in a different superposition, at ⌊log⁡2L⌋=204\lfloor\log_2 L\rfloor = 204⌊log2​L⌋=204 qubits, for every technology. The derivations are verified in Lean 4, with the postulates and the cited physics as named hypotheses.

I. Introduction

Rational Quantum Mechanics (RaQM) [1–4] leaves the Schrödinger equation untouched and instead restricts the bases in which a quantum state is defined: a qubit

∣ψ⟩=cos⁡θ2 ∣1⟩+eiϕsin⁡θ2 ∣−1⟩|\psi\rangle = \cos\tfrac{\theta}{2}\,|1\rangle + e^{i\phi}\sin\tfrac{\theta}{2}\,|{-1}\rangle∣ψ⟩=cos2θ​∣1⟩+eiϕsin2θ​∣−1⟩
(1)

with θ\thetaθ and ϕ\phiϕ the colatitude and azimuth of the state on the Bloch sphere, exists only in bases with

cos⁡2θ2=mL,ϕ2π=nL,\cos^2\tfrac{\theta}{2} = \frac{m}{L},\qquad \frac{\phi}{2\pi} = \frac{n}{L},cos22θ​=Lm​,2πϕ​=Ln​,
(2)

with m∈{0,…,L}m\in\{0,\dots,L\}m∈{0,…,L} and n∈{0,…,L−1}n\in\{0,\dots,L-1\}n∈{0,…,L−1}. The state is then a length-LLL bit string whose fraction of +1+1+1 entries is cos⁡2(θ/2)\cos^2(\theta/2)cos2(θ/2) and whose cyclic shift by nnn places is the phase [2]. Born’s rule becomes a matter of counting. Bell’s inequality is evaded because, by Niven’s theorem [5], the counterfactual measurement settings its derivation requires are not permitted bases [3, 6]. And the number NNN of qubits in a random state has a ceiling: Palmer bounds it by counting bits, 2N+1−2≤NL2^{N+1} - 2 \le NL2N+1−2≤NL [2, 4]. This paper instead counts the room on the last qubit’s string (Sec. IV A): each of the 2N−12^{N-1}2N−1 joint outcomes of the other qubits needs two of its LLL cells, so a random state needs 2N≤L2^N \le L2N≤L, and

Nmax⁡=⌊log⁡2L⌋,N_{\max} = \lfloor\log_2 L\rfloor ,Nmax​=⌊log2​L⌋,
(3)

beyond which, as Palmer argues, quantum algorithms that spread their state across all of Hilbert space lose their exponential advantage [2].

Palmer fixes LLL from gravity. State reduction is a chaotic shift map that lowers LLL by one each Planck time tP=ℏG/c5t_P = \sqrt{\hbar G/c^5}tP​=ℏG/c5​, so the reduction time is τ∗=(L−1)tP\tau^* = (L-1)t_Pτ∗=(L−1)tP​. Equating this to the Diósi–Penrose collapse time ℏ/EG\hbar/E_Gℏ/EG​ [7, 8] gives

L=⌈EPEG⌉,L = \left\lceil\frac{E_P}{E_G}\right\rceil ,L=⌈EG​EP​​⌉,
(4)

where EP=ℏ/tPE_P = \hbar/t_PEP​=ℏ/tP​ is the Planck energy, EGE_GEG​ is the gravitational self-energy of the qubit’s superposition, and ⌈x⌉\lceil x\rceil⌈x⌉ is the smallest integer not less than xxx. Both EPE_PEP​ and EGE_GEG​ contain GGG. Gravity is the input and LLL the output, varying with the qubit from 106410^{64}1064 for a quantum-dot electron to 1010910^{109}10109 for a hyperfine ion-trap qubit [2]. Palmer notes that his Nmax⁡N_{\max}Nmax​ lies near Davies’ cosmological information bound [9] and that this is unlikely to be a coincidence.

We take that remark literally and reverse the causality: LLL does not exist because of gravitation; gravitation exists because of LLL, one universal constant of nature. Table I shows what the reversal yields; the sections below derive each row. We make the reversal concrete with two postulates that put Palmer’s bit string on a ring of cells; the cells and the largest rings, those of LLL cells, are the register. Palmer’s phase operator is a cyclic permutation of the string, each application a rotation by 2π/L2\pi/L2π/L about the polar axis [2], so a full turn of phase takes LLL steps; that those steps are the cells of a ring is not in his construction. A companion preprint builds on the postulates [10]; nothing here depends on it.

Four strands of earlier work meet here. That the Hilbert space of a region with a horizon is finite, with Λ\LambdaΛ setting its dimension, was argued by Banks [11] and by Bao, Carroll, and Singh [12]; that Hilbert space itself may be discrete, by Buniy, Hsu, and Zee [13, 14]. That Einstein’s equations are an equation of state of horizon entropy is Jacobson’s [15, 16], developed by Padmanabhan [17, 18] and Verlinde [19, 20]. The holographic principle [21–23] supplies the area law these arguments rest on, and holographic dark energy [24, 25] ties the vacuum’s energy to the horizon’s area. That the acceleration scale of galaxies is of order cH0cH_0cH0​ is Milgrom’s observation [26, 27], which the radial acceleration relation has sharpened [28, 29]. And the bound on the universe’s information [9, 30] is the strand Palmer’s remark names. This paper joins them with one integer: LLL fixes the count of the register, which gives the area law and the horizon’s entropy, and LLL itself gives the ceiling.

Figure 1 shows the derivation, which runs one way. The postulates fix the count of the register, L2/4−L/2+1L^2/4 - L/2 + 1L2/4−L/2+1 largest rings. A largest ring, LLL cells of length ℓc\lcℓc​, is a closed geodesic of space, a circle of radius RΛ=Lℓc/2π\RL = L\lc/2\piRΛ​=Lℓc​/2π. Every observer at rest, in the sense of Sec. II, has a cosmological horizon, a sphere of that radius (Sec. IV D). The horizon is thermal and holds one bit for each of the register’s largest rings. From that entropy, thermodynamics, and the cited geometry of Sec. III follow Einstein’s equations, with GGG in terms of the cell, so the measured GGG fixes the cell. The solution of Einstein’s equations without a mass gives every observer’s horizon the radius of the largest ring, which ties Λ\LambdaΛ to LLL, so the measured Λ\LambdaΛ gives LLL. The cell and LLL are the framework’s two constants; those two measurements fix them, nothing is adjusted, and Table I marks the rows where they enter. Beyond those two measurements, the galactic scale gives LLL a second time, through a0a_0a0​, the scale of the radial acceleration relation, which Sec. IV C derives from the strings that carry a body’s information, with equipartition and maximum entropy. The strings’ energies are spread at the horizon’s temperature, so a string’s energy is on average one thermal energy of the horizon; the vacuum’s heat is the fraction ln⁡2\ln2ln2 of that average (Sec. IV E). The qubit ceiling, which needs no input from gravity, must find the same LLL. The count, its relations under the stated inputs, and every number computed from them are machine-checked in Lean 4 (Data availability).

II. Postulates and Count

Two postulates define the register. A ring is a closed line of translation in space; a cell is a place on a ring, holding one bit of each ring through it; a tick is the time tc\tctc​ that light takes to cross a cell, and time runs one way, from each tick to the next; a largest ring is a ring of LLL cells, the most a ring has (Postulate 1), and the register is the cells and the largest rings; a qubit is a two-level quantum system, whatever realizes it. A state is given up to a factor eiγe^{i\gamma}eiγ on all its amplitudes, for one qubit those of Eq. (1); γ\gammaγ is the state’s global phase, and multiplying a state by eiΔe^{i\Delta}eiΔ changes its global phase by Δ\DeltaΔ. A state that one tick multiplies by e−iΔe^{-i\Delta}e−iΔ has energy ℏΔ/tc\hbar\Delta/\tcℏΔ/tc​, as in quantum mechanics, where a state of energy EEE gains the factor e−iEt/ℏe^{-iEt/\hbar}e−iEt/ℏ in the time ttt.

Postulate 1 (the register). Every physical law and quantity is defined by qubits, and quantum mechanics is granular. A state is a linear combination of outcomes of its qubits. Every qubit is a string of bits, one on each cell of a ring, each cell of length ℓc\lcℓc​, which light crosses in one tick. No ring has more than LLL cells, with L∈NL\in\mathbb{N}L∈N. The bits are the possible outcomes of one measurement of the qubit, and the string’s cyclic position on its ring is the qubit’s phase. Any two qubits can be measured jointly. The shift moves every bit of a string one cell along its ring per tick; whatever else a tick does to a string’s bits is an interaction. The global phase of a state is hidden: no law depends on its value.

Postulate 2 (the rings). Every cell has one opposite, the same cell halfway around every largest ring through it. Any two cells not opposite lie on exactly one largest ring, any two largest rings share a cell, and no ring holds every cell. No cell differs from another: some map of the cells that keeps the largest rings carries any cell to any other and leaves every law unchanged. No law depends on the direction in which a ring passes through a cell. Every largest ring is a closed geodesic of space, made of its cells as segments of length ℓc\lcℓc​.

By the definition of a cell, every ring carries exactly one string: each of its cells holds one bit of it, and those bits form a string of Postulate 1. We do not assume the length of a cell, ℓc\lcℓc​: Sec. III derives GGG in terms of it, and the measured GGG then fixes it at πln⁡2\sqrt{\pi\ln2}πln2​ Planck lengths, to leading order in 1/L1/L1/L. The tick is then tc=ℓc/c\tc = \lc/ctc​=ℓc​/c, and the cell’s units of energy, mass, and acceleration are Ec=ℏc/ℓc\Ec = \hbar c/\lcEc​=ℏc/ℓc​, mc=ℏ/cℓc\mc = \hbar/c\lcmc​=ℏ/cℓc​, and ac=c2/ℓc\ac = c^2/\lcac​=c2/ℓc​, so that a mass MMM is α=M/mc\alpha = M/\mcα=M/mc​ cell masses. LLL ticks of the shift make one lap of a largest ring: the lap time is LtcL\tcLtc​. From here on, a ring is a largest ring unless it is called shorter.

The horizon’s area. A largest ring is LLL cells of length ℓc\lcℓc​, and by Postulate 2 a closed geodesic made of them as segments, of length LℓcL\lcLℓc​. Let RΛ\RLRΛ​ be the radius of a circle of that length,

RΛ=L ℓc2π;\RL = \frac{L\,\lc}{2\pi} ;RΛ​=2πLℓc​​;
(5)

Sec. IV D derives that each largest ring is such a circle and that every observer at rest has a cosmological horizon, a sphere of the same radius, of area Ahor=4πRΛ2=L2ℓc2/πA_{\rm hor} = 4\pi\RL^2 = L^2\lc^2/\piAhor​=4πRΛ2​=L2ℓc2​/π. That derivation solves Einstein’s equations without a mass and uses their form, not the value of the entropy density that this area fixes in Sec. III. In the terms defined above, space is the cells of the rings: by the last sentence of Postulate 2 each cell is a segment of length ℓc\lcℓc​ of a closed geodesic, so a length along a ring is a number of cells, and the manifold, the smooth space in which a horizon is a sphere (Sec. IV D), describes that space at the scale of lengths and areas. The same sentence matches the register on pairs of cells: two cells that are not opposite lie on exactly one largest ring (Postulate 2), as two points that are not antipodal lie on exactly one great circle of the three-sphere, which Sec. IV D finds space to be. Postulate 2 names space, so the manifold is given with the postulates.

What the manifold contributes. We relate the two through the largest rings, each a closed geodesic of space (Postulate 2), and through their count. Rest and acceleration are the manifold’s descriptions of a body. In the manifold, an observer or a body at rest is unaccelerated, and the geometry about it does not change in time. The horizon counted here is that of an observer at rest in the solution without a mass (Sec. IV D); the horizons of different observers differ in place, not in radius or count, since Postulate 2 distinguishes no cell. For an observer at rest, the manifold describes the register’s incidence, that is, which rings share a cell, only for the rings through his cell. These rings are closed geodesics through his place, and they meet again at the opposite of his cell, the same cell halfway around each of them (Postulate 2). The manifold holds the register one cell at a time, the rings through a cell with their cells along them, and the derivation uses nothing more of its incidence. The count and the horizon share a number: the horizon counts all RRR largest rings (below), each worth Ahor/RA_{\rm hor}/RAhor​/R of its area, and every largest ring has half its cells inside any observer’s horizon (Sec. IV C). That is all the horizon’s geometry contributes: the count never uses the places of cells. A state is a linear combination of outcomes of its qubits (Postulate 1): a body is strings of bits on rings, and its rings are largest rings of the register (Sec. IV D).

The count. Postulate 2 fixes the number of cells and of largest rings, and this count is the new input to gravity. An opposite lies halfway around a ring of LLL cells, so LLL is even. Take a largest ring, which exists by the definition of LLL as the most cells a ring has, a cell XXX off it, which exists since no ring holds every cell, and a cell YYY on it. The opposite of YYY lies on the ring, so XXX and YYY are not opposite and lie on one largest ring, which holds the opposites of both as well. These four cells are distinct, since XXX and with it its opposite are off the first ring, while YYY and its opposite are on it, so L≥4L\ge4L≥4. Every largest ring through a cell PPP passes through its opposite P′P'P′, and two rings through PPP share only PPP and P′P'P′, since two cells not opposite fix one ring. So the rings through PPP cut the remaining cells into disjoint sets, one for each ring, of L−2L-2L−2 cells each. Any two largest rings share a cell (Postulate 2), and with it its opposite. Take a largest ring AAA through PPP, which exists since PPP and any cell not opposite it lie on one (Postulate 2), and a cell QQQ off it (Postulate 2). With SSS a cell of AAA other than PPP and P′P'P′, the cells QQQ and SSS are not opposite, since the opposite of SSS lies on AAA, so one largest ring EEE passes through both. It misses PPP, since the one ring through PPP and SSS is AAA, which does not hold QQQ; and it misses P′P'P′, since the opposite of P′P'P′ is PPP. Each ring through PPP meets EEE in one opposite pair, distinct rings in distinct pairs, and every pair of EEE lies on a ring through PPP; EEE has L/2L/2L/2 pairs, so ρ=L/2\rho = L/2ρ=L/2 rings pass through every cell. Every cell not opposite PPP lies on one of them, so the register has

C=2+ρ(L−2)=L22−L+2 cells,R=CρL=L24−L2+1 largest rings,\begin{split} C &= 2 + \rho(L-2) = \frac{L^2}{2} - L + 2 \ \text{cells},\\ R &= \frac{C\rho}{L} = \frac{L^2}{4} - \frac{L}{2} + 1 \ \text{largest rings}, \end{split}CR​=2+ρ(L−2)=2L2​−L+2 cells,=LCρ​=4L2​−2L​+1 largest rings,​
(6)

and C=2RC = 2RC=2R: one ring for every opposite pair of cells. With a cell and its opposite taken as a point and a largest ring as a line, the register is a finite projective plane of order L/2−1L/2 - 1L/2−1 (for L≥6L\ge6L≥6), with RRR points and RRR lines. That constrains LLL: every known plane has prime-power order, and Bruck and Ryser exclude many others [31]; by the clause of Postulate 2 that no cell differs from another, the plane must also have symmetries that carry any point to any other. Neither the postulates nor RaQM, which takes L∈NL\in\mathbb{N}L∈N with no further restriction [2], limits LLL otherwise. Conversely, for every prime power kkk the plane over the field of kkk elements [32] has a symmetry that runs through all its points in one cycle [33]. Doubling its points gives a register of L=2(k+1)L = 2(k+1)L=2(k+1) with the incidence that Postulate 2 asks for. It also has maps of the cells that keep the rings and carry any cell to any other, the register’s part of what Postulate 2 asks for; the Lean files prove both. So a register exists within the percent or so to which the measured Λ\LambdaΛ fixes LLL (Appendix A): for instance, 522895228952289 is prime, so k=5228913k = 52289^{13}k=5228913 gives L=2(k+1)=4.36882×1061L = 2(k+1) = 4.36882\times10^{61}L=2(k+1)=4.36882×1061, which lies within it, as the Lean files check. Such values are dense: near this LLL, about one even LLL in 141141141 has L/2−1L/2-1L/2−1 prime [34], some 3×10573\times10^{57}3×1057 of them within a percent. To leading order in 1/L1/L1/L, a ring’s share of the horizon’s area is Ahor/R=4ℓc2/πA_{\rm hor}/R = 4\lc^2/\piAhor​/R=4ℓc2​/π.

The entropy. A horizon’s entropy counts what can change in the strings that describe it, those that define its physical laws, and by Postulate 1 all strings together do. Every ring carries one string (above). The shift (Postulate 1) is a translation along the ring, and a translation along a ring can go two ways, with the ring or against it: the two senses. No law fixes the sense, since none depends on the direction in which a ring passes through a cell (Postulate 2), so the sense is a property of the string’s state, and reading it is a measurement with two values. The horizon is that of an observer at rest, and so are its strings: each is one qubit, with two outcomes and a phase (Postulate 1), and the measurement whose outcomes its bits are is the reading of the sense: by definition, a bit 111 is the sense with the ring and a bit −1-1−1 the sense against it (the doublet of Ref. [10]). A string with mmm 1s is a superposition of the two senses, and m/Lm/Lm/L is the probability of the sense with the ring, Eq. (2); its cyclic position, the qubit’s phase (Postulate 1), is the relative phase of the two. A string of one sense has the same bit on every cell, so the shift leaves it as it is, up to its global phase (Postulate 1), and that phase changes alike in either sense, since no law depends on the ring’s direction (Postulate 2). The tick is linear, since a state is a linear combination of outcomes (Postulate 1), so it multiplies every superposition of the two senses by that one phase. So no bit moves and no free tick changes the relative phase: what changes from tick to tick is the global phase. By the definition of energy (above) the global phase decreases by Etc/ℏE\tc/\hbarEtc​/ℏ per tick for a string of energy EEE. The companion preprint [10] leaves that energy open, and Sec. IV E finds its average. A string is free between interactions (below). Interactions change the states of the strings but not their number; a companion preprint treats them [35], and nothing here rests on it. Between interactions all the mass and light of the universe consists of strings on their rings, and the count is of these strings. What interactions do to the count is not derived here. Where the later sections count the strings about a body, its matter stays put rather than radiating away, so its strings interact rarely and the counts neglect their interactions. The early universe, where interactions are not rare, enters only through the bit’s history below. Since a string’s two outcomes have one energy, in the horizon’s thermal state (Sec. III) the string is maximally mixed: either sense has the probability 1/21/21/2, the string holds one bit, kBln⁡2k_B\ln2kB​ln2, the most a qubit holds, and half the bits of a string in that state are 111s on average. That state leaves the string’s position, the phase, free. The strings are free, and the thermal state of free systems is the product of their own thermal states (thermodynamics), so their entropies add. A horizon’s entropy is therefore one bit for each ring of the register: the horizon of an observer at rest holds

ShorkB=Rln⁡2=L24ln⁡2\frac{S_{\rm hor}}{k_B} = R\ln2 = \frac{L^2}{4}\ln2kB​Shor​​=Rln2=4L2​ln2
(7)

to leading order. It comes from the register’s count, not from Bekenstein and Hawking, and equals their quarter per Planck area once GGG fixes the cell (Sec. III).

The bit’s history. Any bath, not only the horizon, weights the two senses equally, since their energy is the same at every temperature. The early universe was such a bath, as the blackbody spectrum of the cosmic microwave background shows [36]. In that bath, photons and charged particles scatter about once per ℏ/αe2kBT\hbar/\alpha_{\rm e}^2k_BTℏ/αe2​kB​T, with αe\alpha_{\rm e}αe​ the fine-structure constant [37]. One scattering leaves either sense equally likely, and the fraction of strings not yet scattered after ttt such times is e−te^{-t}e−t, so after ln⁡R≈282\ln R\approx282lnR≈282 of them fewer than one of the RRR strings is out of equilibrium; at kBT=1k_BT = 1kB​T=1 MeV, about a second after the start [38], that is 3.5×10−153.5\times10^{-15}3.5×10−15 s. Every string has kept its bit since: an interaction changes its sense without making either likelier, and no law favors a sense (Postulate 2).

The symmetry of space. Two clauses of Postulate 2 say that some map of the cells that keeps the largest rings carries any cell to any other and leaves every law unchanged, and that no law depends on the direction in which a ring passes through a cell. Every law is defined by qubits (Postulate 1), a function of the register, so by the two clauses it is the same at every cell of every ring. In the manifold a ring runs along a closed geodesic of space (Postulate 2), and a law at a place of space, in a direction there, is the law on a ring that runs there. A place or direction that no ring could run through would be a part of space the strings do not describe, against Postulate 1, so a ring can run through any place in any direction. Every law is therefore the same at every place and in every direction: the symmetry of space. Without a mass, every string is in the same thermal state, and each of its cells holds one of the LLL possible outcomes of its measurement (Postulate 1). The strings are free, so in that state no string is correlated with another (above), and the state is the same everywhere too. Section III uses the symmetry on every local horizon, and Sec. IV D uses it for the solution without a mass.

Counting in the bulk. On the horizon of the solution without a mass the count is exact, one string for each ring (above). A sphere of radius rrr about a body holds the strings that cross its surface, and its entropy is one bit for each string, its sense, as on a horizon. The register alone does not count them. Along the L/2L/2L/2 rings through the body’s cell it has LLL cells at every distance short of the opposite cell (Sec. IV C), and it puts half of every ring inside the horizon, but it does not say which rings enter a smaller sphere. The manifold decides which strings a sphere holds. Without a mass, the solution’s space at an instant is a three-sphere of radius RΛ\RLRΛ​ (Sec. IV D), and the largest rings at that instant, closed geodesics of that space by Postulate 2, are great circles of it. This drawing of the rings as great circles keeps the rings, with their cells as arcs of length ℓc\lcℓc​. It does not show which cells two rings share, except for the rings through an observer’s cell (above). A ring with a point inside a sphere smaller than the horizon also has one outside, the antipode of that point, so it crosses the sphere’s surface; the sphere holds one string for each ring that enters it. A great circle enters a sphere of areal radius rrr, the rrr for which the sphere’s area is 4πr24\pi r^24πr2, exactly when the circle’s distance from the sphere’s center is less than the sphere’s geodesic radius. The points that close to a great circle take the fraction (r/RΛ)2(r/\RL)^2(r/RΛ​)2 of the three-sphere (Archimedes’ hat-box theorem in four dimensions). Every law and quantity is defined by qubits (Postulate 1), so the drawing is no part of the state and no rotation of it is preferred: the rotations are weighted by a weighting that no rotation changes, which is the uniform one, by the uniqueness of Haar measure. Turning the drawing moves a given point the other way relative to the rings, so the rotations spread the point evenly over the three-sphere. So each ring crosses a sphere about the point for the fraction (r/RΛ)2(r/\RL)^2(r/RΛ​)2 of the rotations, and the average count is the number of rings times (r/RΛ)2(r/\RL)^2(r/RΛ​)2 for every drawing: the state fixes it. Ns(r)N_s(r)Ns​(r) is that average. With the RRR rings of Eq. (6), L2/4L^2/4L2/4 to leading order in 1/L1/L1/L, and with n=r/ℓcn = r/\lcn=r/ℓc​ the areal radius in cells,

Ns(r)=L24(rRΛ)2=π2n2.N_s(r) = \frac{L^2}{4}\Big(\frac{r}{\RL}\Big)^2 = \pi^2 n^2 .Ns​(r)=4L2​(RΛ​r​)2=π2n2.
(8)

This is the area law of a screen, a closed surface whose entropy is read from its area as a horizon’s is [17, 19]. Here it is derived: one string on average for each ring’s share of the area, 4ℓc2/π4\lc^2/\pi4ℓc2​/π, on every sphere no larger than the horizon, in accord with the symmetry of space. Sections III and IV C use it as the count on spheres about a body, the count without a mass, and find how a mass lowers it. Two distances are in play. The register’s is counted in cells along a ring, and it is proper distance, since a largest ring is a closed geodesic made of its cells as segments of length ℓc\lcℓc​ (Postulate 2); Sec. IV C uses it for the distance to the horizon along a ring. The manifold’s is the areal radius, which Eq. (8) uses for the number of the sphere’s strings. For r≪RΛr\ll\RLr≪RΛ​ the two agree, and at the horizon they are L/4L/4L/4 and L/2πL/2\piL/2π cells; each is used where it is exact (Secs. IV C and IV D). Areas, light cones, and the Raychaudhuri equation are written as in Jacobson’s argument (Sec. III); the register constructs no manifold and adds only the count.

Equation (8) is the average count without a mass. For an observer at rest on the sphere or inside it, the L/2L/2L/2 rings through his cell pass through his place (above), so they are not turned with the rest of the drawing; the other rings, whose position relative to his place is no part of the state, keep the average. Each of his rings counts at most once, whereas the average gives it the weight (r/RΛ)2(r/\RL)^2(r/RΛ​)2. So his count exceeds the average by at most (L/2)(1−r2/RΛ2)(L/2)(1 - r^2/\RL^2)(L/2)(1−r2/RΛ2​), which is at most the fraction RΛℓc/πr2\RL\lc/\pi r^2RΛ​ℓc​/πr2 of Ns(r)N_s(r)Ns​(r), 1.3×10−91.3\times10^{-9}1.3×10−9 at r=1r = 1r=1 m. Section IV C treats the body as a point, on spheres far larger than it.

The reversal. We keep Palmer’s picture of state reduction as a shift map, one step per tick by Postulate 1, so that τ∗=Ltc\tau^* = L\tcτ∗=Ltc​, but with LLL universal. With LLL a constant of nature the map cannot lower it; the reversal keeps only its clock, LLL ticks. Then, by Eq. (5),

τ∗=L tc=2πRΛc,\tau^* = L\,\tc = \frac{2\pi\RL}{c} ,τ∗=Ltc​=c2πRΛ​​,
(9)

the lap time of a largest ring, 2π/H∞2\pi/H_\infty2π/H∞​ with H∞=c/RΛH_\infty = c/\RLH∞​=c/RΛ​. In Palmer’s argument the energy that goes with a reduction time is ℏ\hbarℏ over it, so the energy that takes the place of EGE_GEG​ is

EcL=ℏτ∗=ℏc2πRΛ=kBTdS,\frac{\Ec}{L} = \frac{\hbar}{\tau^*} = \frac{\hbar c}{2\pi\RL} = k_B T_{\rm dS},LEc​​=τ∗ℏ​=2πRΛ​ℏc​=kB​TdS​,
(10)

with TdST_{\rm dS}TdS​ the Gibbons–Hawking temperature of a horizon of radius RΛ\RLRΛ​ [39]. Palmer’s Eq. (4), read backward, says that gravity’s characteristic energy in the reduction process is the thermal energy of the cosmological horizon, the same for every qubit. No derivation below uses that relation: Sec. IV E finds this value from thermodynamics, as the average of the strings’ energies, which differ from string to string. Three consequences of the reversal follow at once. First, τ∗∼1011\tau^*\sim10^{11}τ∗∼1011 yr, so an isolated qubit never completes reduction; Palmer makes the same observation. Second, LLL no longer depends on the qubit, so Nmax⁡N_{\max}Nmax​ is the same for every technology, which is the sharpest experimental difference between the two causal orderings. Third, the reversal discards mass-dependent gravitational collapse, which Palmer’s program takes to be gravity’s role in quantum mechanics [40]. Here every system shares the same clock, so the definiteness of macroscopic bodies is not supplied by gravity and must come, as in standard quantum theory, from environmental decoherence. The reversed theory therefore predicts no mass-dependent collapse signal of Diósi–Penrose type. The null result of the underground search of Ref. [41] agrees with it and, since Palmer’s shift map is non-dissipative, with his ordering too, so the search does not discriminate between them.

III. Newton’s Constant from the Count

We derive GGG from the count of Sec. II and the horizon’s area (Sec. IV D), with thermodynamics and cited geometry. Beyond the postulates the paper takes three sources, none of them a number. Thermodynamics: a horizon is thermal with the temperature of its period, and the energy that crosses it is heat; these two inputs hold for every local horizon (this section) and for the cosmological horizon (Sec. IV D). There the strings are in the thermal state at the horizon’s temperature, which for free strings is the product of their own thermal states (Sec. II). The energies the strings hold are spread at that temperature and, for matter that stays put, do not change (Sec. IV E). Thermodynamics also gives the first law, for every small region and every observer (this section) and for the cosmic fluid (Sec. VI), and the Deser–Levin temperature (Sec. IV C). For the galactic law it gives equipartition and, through the principle of maximum entropy, the Gibbs distribution of the strings’ energies (Secs. IV C, IV E). Quantum mechanics: the gates, which act on what the register holds as on any state (Sec. IV A). With the Porter–Thomas distribution of a random state’s probabilities, cited there, the gates give the bound on the return above the ceiling. What the paper takes from general relativity is no law of it but mathematics, cited, each theorem with its inputs derived here, taken from the postulates, or stated as conditions. From Lorentzian geometry on the manifold Postulate 2 names [42–44]: this section uses the Raychaudhuri equation, the contracted Bianchi identity, the static weak field, and the Leibniz rule for the divergence of a flow’s stress tensor; Sec. IV C uses that rule again, with the Newtonian limit of geodesic motion; and Sec. IV D uses the curvature of a static, spherically symmetric metric, from which it derives the Schwarzschild–de Sitter solution, and Einstein’s constraint on the space at an instant. From Riemannian geometry of the space at an instant [45, 46]: Schur’s lemma and the Hopf–Rinow and Killing–Hopf theorems (Sec. IV D). That the space at an instant is the three-sphere, whose closed geodesics are its great circles, Sec. IV D derives. Of the Schwarzschild–de Sitter solution it reads off the surface gravity of its horizons and the limit up to which it has them. The Misner–Sharp energy of the horizon (Sec. IV D) and Komar’s energy (Sec. III C) are definitions, evaluated on the derived solution; the perihelion and deflection formulas (Sec. IV B) enter as numbers only. The symmetry of space is not among them: Sec. II derives it. Postulate 1’s first sentence is applied to the geometry of space, to space, to the entropy of the cosmological horizon and of a local horizon, to the count about a body, to a body’s energy, which the strings that carry its information hold, to mass energy, which is counted in bits, and to the energy inside the horizon (Sec. II, this section, Secs. IV C, IV D, IV E), each time as the sentence itself; the Lean files carry each application as a named hypothesis. Two observations enter as well: the hot early universe, in the bit’s history of Sec. II, and the three dimensions of space (Sec. IV D).

Two things enter the balance of heat and entropy. A horizon is thermal: its state is periodic in imaginary time, and a state with imaginary-time period τ\tauτ has temperature kBT=ℏ/τk_BT = \hbar/\taukB​T=ℏ/τ, which is the Kubo–Martin–Schwinger condition [47, 48]. The period of a horizon is 2πc/a2\pi c/a2πc/a, with aaa its surface gravity, which is the content of the Unruh and Gibbons–Hawking temperatures [39, 49]; for a horizon of radius RΛ\RLRΛ​ it is the lap time of a largest ring, Eq. (9). The energy that crosses a horizon is heat, δQ=T dS\delta Q = T\,dSδQ=TdS, which is Jacobson’s step [15]. Jacobson assumes that the entropy per unit area is the same on every horizon. Here the entropy comes from the register, Eq. (7), which fixes that density in units of the cell. The density is a law (below), so by the symmetry of space (Sec. II) it is the same on every horizon. The count adds this to Jacobson’s derivation, in which the density is a free parameter fixed by Newton’s constant (Sec. III C). We do not use Verlinde’s entropic argument for Newton’s law [19], in which a force driven by a screen’s entropy is the contested step [50]; Jacobson’s argument uses no force. Verlinde’s later work reaches the deep regime of galaxies from an elastic response of the entropy [20]; Sec. IV C reaches the whole relation from the strings.

A. The temperature of a horizon in cells

In cells, a horizon whose period is LhL_hLh​ ticks, τ=Lhtc\tau = L_h\tcτ=Lh​tc​, has by the thermal assumption the temperature

kBT=ℏLhtc=EcLh.k_B T = \frac{\hbar}{L_h\tc} = \frac{\Ec}{L_h} .kB​T=Lh​tc​ℏ​=Lh​Ec​​.
(11)

For the horizon of radius RΛ\RLRΛ​ the period is the lap time of a largest ring, Lh=LL_h = LLh​=L, and Eq. (11) is Eq. (10). An observer accelerating at aaa has a horizon c2/ac^2/ac2/a behind him, whose period is 2πc/a2\pi c/a2πc/a, that is, La=2πc2/aℓcL_a = 2\pi c^2/a\lcLa​=2πc2/aℓc​ ticks; Eq. (11) then gives kBTa=ℏa/2πck_BT_a = \hbar a/2\pi ckB​Ta​=ℏa/2πc, Unruh’s temperature. Through every point of spacetime, in every null direction, passes such a horizon, a local Rindler horizon.

B. Clausius relation

A local Rindler horizon is crossed by largest rings, whose cells are segments of the geodesics there (Postulate 2), and its state is a state of those strings (Postulate 1). So its entropy per unit area is a law, and by the symmetry of space it is the cosmological horizon’s (Sec. II), one bit per ring’s share of area; Jacobson’s balance of heat and entropy reads

δQ=Ta dS=kBTaln⁡2 dNs=ℏaln⁡22πc dNs:\delta Q = T_a\,dS = k_BT_a\ln2\,dN_s = \frac{\hbar a\ln2}{2\pi c}\,dN_s :δQ=Ta​dS=kB​Ta​ln2dNs​=2πcℏaln2​dNs​:
(12)

with NsN_sNs​ the number of rings the horizon holds (Sec. II), each ring it gains takes in kBTaln⁡2k_BT_a\ln2kB​Ta​ln2, its temperature times one bit of entropy, which is Landauer’s energy of a bit [51]. Energy crossing a horizon therefore adds rings, 2πc/(ℏaln⁡2)2\pi c/(\hbar a\ln2)2πc/(ℏaln2) of them per unit of energy, and with a ring’s share of area 4ℓc2/π4\lc^2/\pi4ℓc2​/π it adds area dA=[8ℓc2c/(ℏaln⁡2)] δQdA = [8\lc^2 c/(\hbar a\ln2)]\,\delta QdA=[8ℓc2​c/(ℏaln2)]δQ. The Raychaudhuri equation gives the change of area in terms of the Ricci tensor, and the balance can hold in every direction at every point, with the first law, only if

Rμν−12Rλλ gμν+Λgμν=2πkBℏc η Tμν,R_{\mu\nu} - \tfrac12 R^{\lambda}{}_{\lambda}\,g_{\mu\nu} + \Lambda g_{\mu\nu} = \frac{2\pi k_B}{\hbar c\,\eta}\,T_{\mu\nu},Rμν​−21​Rλλ​gμν​+Λgμν​=ℏcη2πkB​​Tμν​,
(13)

with η\etaη the entropy per unit area. The balance fixes Eq. (13) only up to a term proportional to the metric, since a stress tensor proportional to the metric has no flux through a null surface and so never enters Eq. (12) [15, 52]. The first law fixes that term. Energy is neither made nor lost in a small region, only carried across its boundary, so for an observer at rest in a local inertial frame the divergence of the energy current vanishes, (∇μTμν)uν=0(\nabla^\mu T_{\mu\nu})u^\nu = 0(∇μTμν​)uν=0. This holds for every four-velocity uuu, so ∇μTμν=0\nabla^\mu T_{\mu\nu} = 0∇μTμν​=0. With the contracted Bianchi identity [42], the coefficient of the term is then one constant, Λ\LambdaΛ, and Eq. (13) holds as written, with matter and without, wherever each ring that a horizon gains takes in one Landauer energy (Sec. IV C). In the static weak field of matter at rest the balance gives ∇2Φ=(πkBc3/ℏη) ρ\nabla^2\Phi = (\pi k_Bc^3/\hbar\eta)\,\rho∇2Φ=(πkB​c3/ℏη)ρ, which is Newton’s law, ∇2Φ=4πGρ\nabla^2\Phi = 4\pi G\rho∇2Φ=4πGρ, with G=c3kB/4ℏηG = c^3k_B/4\hbar\etaG=c3kB​/4ℏη [42]. Nothing in this is a force: Eq. (13) is a condition on the geometry, that the count of every local horizon stays in balance with the heat that crosses it. The same conservation moves matter and light on the geodesics of that geometry. For dust, whose stress tensor is ρuμuν\rho u_\mu u_\nuρuμ​uν​, it gives uμ∇μuν=0u^\mu\nabla_\mu u_\nu = 0uμ∇μ​uν​=0 [42]. Light crosses a cell in one tick in every direction (Postulates 1 and 2), so it moves at ccc and its rays are null. For light whose energy moves with it along its ray, for every observer, the stress tensor is ρkμkν\rho k_\mu k_\nuρkμ​kν​, with kkk the tangent of the ray, and conservation makes its rays null geodesics. A small body also moves on a geodesic [53], a result that no derivation here uses.

with ℓP≡ℏG/c3\ell_P \equiv \sqrt{\hbar G/c^3}ℓP​≡ℏG/c3​, so the Planck length is a derived quantity, the cell over πln⁡2\sqrt{\pi\ln2}πln2​. So Newton’s law reads: the body’s energy is shared equally by the Ns(r)N_s(r)Ns​(r) strings that any sphere around it holds on average; the share per string is set by the Unruh temperature of the pull, which an observer held on the sphere sees where the pull far exceeds the push and the horizon’s surface gravity; and the share falls as 1/r21/r^21/r2, since the number of strings grows as r2r^2r2. Two remarks follow. First, where Jacobson leaves η\etaη free, here it is a count, one bit per ring’s share of area, πkBln⁡2/4ℓc2\pi k_B\ln2/4\lc^2πkB​ln2/4ℓc2​, so the measured GGG fixes the cell, the largest ring ties GGG to LLL and to Λ\LambdaΛ (Sec. IV D), and the same LLL caps a quantum computer (Sec. IV A). Without cells there is no count, and η\etaη stays free. Section IV C finds how the share changes when not every string of the sphere carries the body’s information. Second, Eq. (14) scales as 1/L21/L^21/L2: with LLL a constant of nature and one bit per ring, GGG is constant exactly when the horizon radius is; this singles out the de Sitter horizon (Sec. IV D) and makes the constancy of GGG and of Λ\LambdaΛ one statement (Sec. VI).

IV. Gravitational Phenomena Scale by Scale

At each gravitational scale the derivation uses one structure of the register, and we record what each scale pins. At the solar scale it is the sphere of Eq. (8); at the galactic scale the string, whose ring runs from the sphere to the horizon; at the cosmological scale the closed ring.

A. Quantum scale: qubits and their ceiling

Probabilities need no further postulate. The bits of a string are the LLL possible outcomes of one measurement of its qubit (Postulate 1), so the probability of the outcome 111 is the share of the bits that are 111, their number over LLL: Eq. (2) holds. Strings measured jointly have their bits paired position by position (below). In Palmer’s state a later string also has a phase for each joint outcome of the earlier ones: a cyclic permutation, in a reference arrangement, of its bits paired with that outcome [2].

On this scale LLL acts directly, through Eq. (3), and the joint measurement of Postulate 1 shows which states it limits. A joint measurement is one measurement, so its possible outcomes are the LLL positions, the same on every string of the qubits it measures: the LLL cells, read at one tick (Postulate 1). The outcome at a position is the bits there. So every position of a later string comes paired with one outcome of the earlier qubits, their bits there. This pairing defines measured jointly, and it is Palmer’s state of NNN qubits, NNN correlated strings of LLL bits with one permutation applied to all of them [2]. It does not require the strings to share a cell, and it is all that the count below uses. The cells of a later string whose bits are paired with one joint outcome of the earlier qubits form a block of the string, and blocks of different outcomes are disjoint. The fraction of 1s on a block is the probability of the outcome 1 given the block’s joint outcome, and the probability of a joint outcome is the product, string by string, of the frequencies of its bits on its blocks. The block’s phase (above) is the later qubit’s phase given that outcome, counted from its string’s position; the count does not use it. A block whose fraction lies strictly between 0 and 1 needs at least two cells, one reading 111 and one reading −1-1−1. In a random state, each of the 2N−12^{N-1}2N−1 joint outcomes of the first N−1N-1N−1 qubits occurs, and given it the last qubit’s bit is 1 with probability strictly between 0 and 1. Its string then needs 2N−12^{N-1}2N−1 blocks of at least two cells, so 2N2^N2N is at most its length, and 2N≤L2^N\le L2N≤L. On a largest ring of the register, of LLL cells, the ceiling is ⌊log⁡2L⌋=204\lfloor\log_2L\rfloor = 204⌊log2​L⌋=204, with log⁡2L=204.8\log_2L = 204.8log2​L=204.8 (Sec. V); a string on a shorter ring, which Postulate 1 allows, would only lower it, and 2N≤L2^N\le L2N≤L holds in every case. Nor does a mass shorten the rings: a mass inside a horizon shortens that horizon’s circumference (Sec. IV C), not the register’s rings.

The bound is not the random state’s alone. It holds for every state in which all 2N2^N2N joint outcomes occur, since each of them takes at least one of the LLL positions, and a product state of NNN qubits, each in a superposition, is such a state: its last string needs the same 2N−12^{N-1}2N−1 blocks of two cells to show them. A state of the Greenberger–Horne–Zeilinger type escapes it, with two joint outcomes and blocks of fraction 0 or 1, one cell each. Most product states are not held exactly even at small NNN: two qubits prepared apart, with the fractions m1/Lm_1/Lm1​/L and m2/Lm_2/Lm2​/L, have the joint frequency m1m2/L2m_1m_2/L^2m1​m2​/L2 for the outcome (1,1)(1,1)(1,1), a multiple of 1/L1/L1/L only when LLL divides m1m2m_1m_2m1​m2​. Postulate 1 fixes each string exactly, its fraction and position, and the pairing only up to its LLL positions; such a state is held with its strings exact and its pairing approximate, and the postulates do not say which pairing. The register therefore holds, at any NNN, something definite in kind: NNN exact strings read in step, in some pairing, with a phase on each block. Where a pairing shows every joint outcome with its frequency, the strings in that pairing, with their blocks’ phases, are the state. This freedom in the pairing does not soften the bound, which is on the pairing itself: no pairing of LLL positions shows more than LLL joint outcomes, so none shows every joint outcome of a state that has more than LLL of them.

Random-circuit sampling has reached 838383 qubits in the published record [57–59] and 103103103 in a manufacturer’s report [60], at cross-entropy fidelities between 0.02%0.02\%0.02% and 1%1\%1%. That is consistent with 2103≤L2^{103}\le L2103≤L, though at those fidelities it does not establish it, and 103103103 is far below log⁡2L=204.8\log_2L = 204.8log2​L=204.8, so this scale does not yet pin LLL. A count of physical qubits, far larger, is not a count of qubits in a random state, and the bound shows nothing in it, for the reason given below. Logical qubits count as physical ones do. Postulate 1 gives a qubit’s bits as the outcomes of one measurement of it, and a logical qubit is a two-level system that comes with its logical measurement, so it has a string (Sec. II). Its bit is read from the bits of the physical qubits that realize it, so their strings must have room for its conditional states as well. In a Calderbank–Shor–Steane code [61, 62] the logical states are equal-weight superpositions of the bit strings in two cosets of a linear code, so a physical bit, given the earlier physical bits, is fixed, balanced, or equal or opposite to the logical bit. The fullest physical string of a random state of NNN logical qubits then has up to 2N2^N2N conditional states to hold, twice as many as a logical string. Where the equal and the opposite case both occur and the 2N2^N2N conditional states are superpositions that all differ in probability, as in a random state, that string needs 2N2^N2N blocks of at least two cells. The ceiling is then 2N+1≤L2^{N+1}\le L2N+1≤L, or 203203203 logical qubits. Below it the encoded state is held with its strings exact and its pairing approximate, as a product state is, even where the joint outcomes of its physical qubits outnumber LLL. Both cases occur in the surface code [63], where the logical bit is the parity of a line of physical bits and all but the last bit of the line take every pattern in both logical states, so the last bit, given the rest of the line, is the logical bit or its opposite. In a repetition code, whose logical states are single bit strings, only the fixed and the equal case occur and the ceiling stays 204204204. The number NNN in the bound counts the qubits of a state, which in the random-circuit test below are logical qubits, and it does not depend on which of them are measured afterward. The 484848 logical qubits demonstrated on 280280280 atoms [64] lie far below the ceiling. On the timescale Palmer gives for factoring tests [2], this scale can measure LLL directly. The test is a random circuit on NNN fault-tolerant logical qubits, deep enough to produce a random state, followed by its inverse. In quantum mechanics the state returns to the initial one with the gate fidelity, the probability of a run without error. Here, once NNN exceeds log⁡2L\log_2Llog2​L, the intermediate state cannot be the random state the circuit calls for, since at least 2N−L2^N - L2N−L of its joint outcomes are missing, a fraction 1−L/2N1 - L/2^N1−L/2N of them: 15% at N=205N = 205N=205 and more than half at 206206206 (Appendix A). No sample shows which outcomes are missing, since a million shots on 205205205 qubits see at most a million of their 22052^{205}2205 outcomes, fewer than one in 105510^{55}1055; the missing outcomes show in the return (below).

The test therefore rests on something else: whether each string has room for the different conditional states of its qubit, its states given the outcomes of the earlier qubits. A block holds the conditional state of its joint outcome, and blocks of different outcomes may hold the same one. In a product state each string has one conditional state to hold, on all its cells (Postulate 1). In a cluster state a qubit’s state depends on the earlier qubits only through the product of the bits of its neighbors among them. Its string has at most two conditional states to hold, one for each value of that product, at every NNN. A stabilizer measurement reads one qubit along XXX, an axis in the equatorial plane of the Bloch sphere, and its neighbors along the polar axis ZZZ. That qubit’s bit is then the product of its neighbors’ bits, and its string again has two conditional states to hold. A state in which each qubit’s state depends on the earlier qubits only through how many of them read −1-1−1 gives a string at most NNN conditional states to hold. RaQM leaves the Schrödinger equation untouched, so these are the conditional states of quantum mechanics, and each string has room for them, two cells for each, at any NNN up to L/2L/2L/2. Each conditional state can then have a block with a cell reading 111 and a cell reading −1-1−1, so the bound on the return (below) does not apply to a state of these kinds. Where the register holds such a state, it returns as in quantum mechanics. In a stabilizer measurement each conditional state is a fixed bit, which a block of any size holds exactly, and a block that holds it shows at every position the product of the neighbors’ bits, as quantum mechanics predicts, at every NNN. Cluster states made on 414414414 qubits [65], and states of the last kind made and undone on some 350350350 atoms [66], therefore do not test that bound.

In the random state the last qubit has a different conditional state, a superposition, for each joint outcome of the others, whatever the order of the strings, and above log⁡2L\log_2Llog2​L its string has too few cells to hold them all. For this state the bound is on what the register holds, so no combination of gates exceeds it: a circuit that calls for a random state of more than log⁡2L\log_2Llog2​L qubits does not produce it. What the register holds instead gives the missing outcomes probability zero, so its overlap with the random state is at most the probability that the random state gives the outcomes that remain. The outcome probabilities of a random state follow the Porter–Thomas distribution [56, 57], under which the lightest fraction fff of the outcomes carries the probability f+(1−f)ln⁡(1−f)f + (1-f)\ln(1-f)f+(1−f)ln(1−f): the lightest 15% carry 1.2%, the lightest 58% carry 21%, so the overlap is at most 0.990.990.99 at N=205N = 205N=205, 0.790.790.79 at 206206206, 0.540.540.54 at 207207207, and 0.120.120.12 at 210210210 (Appendix A). A circuit acts on what the register holds as it acts on any state, an input of Sec. III, so the state returns with at most that fraction of the gate fidelity, an eighth of it at 210210210 qubits. How well the random state returns just below log⁡2L\log_2Llog2​L, where the blocks are a few cells wide (Sec. V), is not derived: the postulates fix the capacity, not which pairing a circuit produces when it calls for more blocks than a string has room for. Error correction does not lift the ceiling, which is set by room and not by errors.

A linear cluster state with one layer of generic rotations reaches the same limit. Rotate each qubit of a linear cluster state of NNN qubits by a generic single-qubit unitary, and measure the first N−1N-1N−1 in the computational basis. In the last qubit the cluster state is (∣CN−1⟩∣0⟩+ZN−1∣CN−1⟩∣1⟩)/2(|C_{N-1}\rangle|0\rangle + Z_{N-1}|C_{N-1}\rangle|1\rangle)/\sqrt2(∣CN−1​⟩∣0⟩+ZN−1​∣CN−1​⟩∣1⟩)/2​, with CN−1C_{N-1}CN−1​ the cluster of the first N−1N-1N−1 qubits, so the ratio of the last qubit’s two amplitudes given the outcomes of the others is rN=(1−t rN−1)/(1+t rN−1)r_N = (1 - t\,r_{N-1})/(1 + t\,r_{N-1})rN​=(1−trN−1​)/(1+trN−1​): rN−1r_{N-1}rN−1​ is the same ratio for qubit N−1N-1N−1 given the outcomes before it, and ttt is one of two numbers, t0t_0t0​ or −1/tˉ0-1/\bar t_0−1/tˉ0​, fixed by the rotation of qubit N−1N-1N−1 and its outcome. From r1=1r_1 = 1r1​=1, each joint outcome gives its own chain of these maps. Each map is one to one, and the two maps give one value only from two earlier values in the ratio −∣t0∣2-|t_0|^2−∣t0​∣2, which generic rotations avoid, as they keep every ratio away from 000 and ∞\infty∞. So the last qubit has a different conditional state, with a probability strictly between 000 and 111, for each of the 2N−12^{N-1}2N−1 joint outcomes, and above 204204204 qubits no string has room for them. The circuit that prepares the state and undoes it is a few gates deep, so the test runs on physical qubits today, though without the bound above, whose Porter–Thomas weights are the random state’s; the devices that made cluster states of 414414414 qubits [65] hold lines of hundreds of qubits.

Magnetic-resonance echo experiments in solids run an evolution that correlates 100100100 to 500050005000 spins and then reverse it, and the return falls as the correlations spread [67–69]. Part of this fall does not shrink when the perturbations that make the reversal inexact are made small [68, 69]. The spins start in a mixed state, for which no count is made here, so these experiments neither show the ceiling nor exclude it. The prediction on this scale is a ceiling of 204204204, or 203203203 logical qubits in the surface code (Sec. VI).

B. Terrestrial and solar scales: the sphere

Einstein’s equations, Eq. (13), have Newton’s law as their weak-field limit, Eq. (16). Gravitational redshift, the perihelion advance of Mercury, light deflection, and gravitational-wave propagation then follow as they do in general relativity [42, 43]. Mercury’s anomalous advance 6πGM⊙/(p c2)6\pi GM_\odot/(p\,c^2)6πGM⊙​/(pc2), with p=aorb(1−e2)p = a_{\rm orb}(1-e^2)p=aorb​(1−e2) the semi-latus rectum of the orbit, is 42.98′′42.98''42.98′′ per century and the deflection of starlight at the solar limb 4GM⊙/(c2R⊙)4GM_\odot/(c^2R_\odot)4GM⊙​/(c2R⊙​) is 1.75′′1.75''1.75′′, both as observed. At the Earth’s orbit, α=1.35×1038\alpha = 1.35\times10^{38}α=1.35×1038 and n=6.27×1045n = 6.27\times10^{45}n=6.27×1045 in Eq. (16) give 5.93×10−35.93\times10^{-3}5.93×10−3 m s−2^{-2}−2. These results depend on LLL and RΛ\RLRΛ​ only through GGG.

This scale therefore pins the cell ℓc=2πRΛ/L\lc = 2\pi\RL/Lℓc​=2πRΛ​/L, and not LLL on its own. The count of a sphere goes as n2n^2n2, with LLL canceled against the unit, Eq. (8); and the horizon of an observer held at solar radii is his own, La≪LL_a\ll LLa​≪L, since a≫c2/RΛa\gg c^2/\RLa≫c2/RΛ​ there. General relativity describes solar-system gravity to exquisite precision, so a theory in which LLL showed up there separately from RΛ\RLRΛ​ would be wrong. The horizon could enter solar-system dynamics by two routes. The horizon’s push on a free body (Sec. IV D) reaches the planets, but with only 5×10−255\times10^{-25}5×10−25 m s−2^{-2}−2 at the Earth’s orbit. For an isolated Sun the law of Sec. IV C departs from Newton’s by the fraction e−h/(1−e−h)e^{-h}/(1-e^{-h})e−h/(1−e−h) with h=gN/a0h = \sqrt{g_N/a_0}h=gN​/a0​​: 3×10−1023\times10^{-102}3×10−102 at Neptune’s orbit, where h=234h = 234h=234, and less inside it; the deep regime begins near GM⊙/a0=7000\sqrt{GM_\odot/a_0} = 7000GM⊙​/a0​​=7000 au. The Sun is not isolated, though. The Galaxy’s field at its position, about 2×10−102\times10^{-10}2×10−10 m s−2^{-2}−2 [70], is of the order of a0a_0a0​. In the field equations of Milgrom’s modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND), where the external field enters the nonlinearity whole, such a field adds a quadrupole to the Sun’s field in the inner solar system, which Cassini’s ranging bounds at Q2=(3±3)×10−27Q_2 = (3\pm3)\times10^{-27}Q2​=(3±3)×10−27 s−2^{-2}−2 [70]. Had the carriers of Sec. IV C sensed the total field, Eq. (24) would be such an equation. Solved numerically for the Sun in a uniform field of 1.6a01.6a_01.6a0​, by the method of Ref. [93], whose values for the simple, standard, and exponential functions it reproduces to 3%, it gives Q2=4×10−26Q_2 = 4\times10^{-26}Q2​=4×10−26 s−2^{-2}−2, twelve standard deviations from Cassini’s value (Data availability). The carriers sense the proper acceleration, which a uniform field does not change (Sec. IV C), so the Galaxy’s field adds only its tide, of order ge/R0≈10−30g_e/R_0 \approx 10^{-30}ge​/R0​≈10−30 s−2^{-2}−2 with R0R_0R0​ the Sun’s distance from the Galactic center, three orders below the bound.

C. Galactic scale: the string

At the scales above, LLL and RΛ\RLRΛ​ entered gravity only through their ratio, and two facts of the register played no part. The strings of a sphere have LLL bits, one on each cell of a largest ring, and reach the horizon. No ring has more than LLL cells, and no observer in de Sitter space sees a horizon colder than Ec/L\Ec/LEc​/L. One held at acceleration aaa sees the two horizons combined in quadrature, kBT=(ℏ/2πc)a2+aΛ2k_BT = (\hbar/2\pi c)\sqrt{a^2 + a_\Lambda^2}kB​T=(ℏ/2πc)a2+aΛ2​​, with aΛa_\LambdaaΛ​ the surface gravity of the de Sitter horizon [71]. That horizon is at RΛ\RLRΛ​ (Sec. IV D), so aΛ=c2/RΛa_\Lambda = c^2/\RLaΛ​=c2/RΛ​ and kBT≥Ec/Lk_BT \ge \Ec/LkB​T≥Ec​/L. The floor is on the temperature, not on the acceleration. Both facts enter at accelerations of order aΛ=cH∞=5.4×10−10a_\Lambda = cH_\infty = 5.4\times10^{-10}aΛ​=cH∞​=5.4×10−10 m s−2^{-2}−2. That the scale at which rotation curves flatten is the horizon’s acceleration, up to a coefficient, is not our result: Milgrom reached it from the Unruh temperature of de Sitter space [72], and Verlinde from its entanglement entropy [20]. Our contribution is the average energy of a string, one thermal energy of the horizon (Sec. IV E), and the strings that carry a body’s information; together they give the law with its coefficient.

A mass draws the horizon in. We begin with the body’s horizon, where the count can be checked against the solution. The solution of Einstein’s equations for a mass MMM at rest inside the cosmological horizon, treated as a point with GM/c2≪RΛGM/c^2\ll\RLGM/c2≪RΛ​, is Schwarzschild–de Sitter [73], with Λ=3/RΛ2\Lambda = 3/\RL^2Λ=3/RΛ2​ at every mass (Sec. IV D). Its outer horizon lies at RΛ−GM/c2\RL - GM/c^2RΛ​−GM/c2 to first order in MMM. By Eq. (15), GM/c2=ℓcα/(πln⁡2)GM/c^2 = \lc\alpha/(\pi\ln2)GM/c2=ℓc​α/(πln2): the mass draws the horizon in by α/(πln⁡2)\alpha/(\pi\ln2)α/(πln2) cells. The horizon’s circumference is LM=L−2α/ln⁡2L_M = L - 2\alpha/\ln2LM​=L−2α/ln2 cells, and the area law (Sec. II), one bit per ring’s share of area, gives it LM2/4L_M^2/4LM2​/4 bits to leading order, the number Eq. (7) would give with LML_MLM​ in place of LLL (the closed geodesics of that length are discussed in Sec. IV D). To first order in MMM the loss is (L/2)⋅(2α/ln⁡2)⋅ln⁡2(L/2)\cdot(2\alpha/\ln2)\cdot\ln2(L/2)⋅(2α/ln2)⋅ln2,

SM=Lα=Mc2kBTdS=2πMcRΛℏ,S_M = L\alpha = \frac{Mc^2}{k_BT_{\rm dS}} = \frac{2\pi Mc\RL}{\hbar} ,SM​=Lα=kB​TdS​Mc2​=ℏ2πMcRΛ​​,

which is Verlinde’s result, Eq. (25) of Ref. [20] (SciPost numbering), in cells; it does not depend on the cell’s size.

Distances from the body. We treat the body as a point, as Newton’s law does. A point is at one place, and a place is a cell (Sec. II); we call the body’s cell the center and draw a sphere of radius rrr about it, with rrr far larger than the body’s size. Postulate 2 gives every other cell a distance from the center: the number of steps between them, the shorter way around, along the one largest ring through both. One cell is an exception: the cell opposite the center lies on every one of the L/2L/2L/2 rings through the center, always L/2L/2L/2 steps away, so its distance is L/2L/2L/2 by any of them. The horizon of a body at rest lies L/4L/4L/4 cells out in the solution without the mass, a quarter of a largest ring, at the proper distance πRΛ/2=Lℓc/4\pi\RL/2 = L\lc/4πRΛ​/2=Lℓc​/4 that Sec. IV D derives. Inside it are the cells nearer to the center than to the center’s opposite. The two cells of an opposite pair lie at the distances ddd and L/2−dL/2 - dL/2−d, one on each side of the horizon or both on it, and every largest ring is made of L/2L/2L/2 such pairs, since it passes through the opposite of each of its cells. So every string has half its cells, L/2L/2L/2 of them, inside the horizon or on it, counting a cell on it as half; Sec. IV D uses this for the horizon’s entropy. The sphere of radius rrr holds on average Ns(r)=π2n2N_s(r) = \pi^2n^2Ns​(r)=π2n2 strings, Eq. (8), counted ring by ring (Sec. II). Each lies on a largest ring, which enters the sphere at one cell and leaves it at another, the string’s two receiving cells, and runs on to the horizon.

The share of a body’s energy. Equation (16) shares the body’s energy equally among the NsN_sNs​ strings of the sphere, two Landauer energies each. The body here is all the mass inside the sphere, so a string’s share is of that total, not of each star within it. Whether every string takes a share is the question. By Postulate 1, energy is held only by strings (Sec. IV E). A string is one qubit (Postulate 1), so it carries the quantum information of the body’s mass, the body’s information for short, at both its receiving cells or at neither. If it carries none, its receiving cells are in the state they have without the body, and the string holds none of the body’s energy there. The body’s energy is therefore shared among the strings that carry its information, and equipartition gives each of them two Landauer energies at the sphere’s temperature, as Eq. (16) does when all of them carry it. Let bbb be the fraction of the sphere’s strings that carry the body’s information, with 0<b≤10 < b \le 10<b≤1. Then

Mc2=2bNs kBTaln⁡2,a=gNb.Mc^2 = 2bN_s\,k_BT_a\ln2 , \qquad a = \frac{g_N}{b} .Mc2=2bNs​kB​Ta​ln2,a=bgN​​.
(18)

Fewer carriers hold the same energy at a higher temperature, and the acceleration is larger. Near the body nearly every string carries the body’s information, b→1b\to1b→1 (below), and Eq. (18) tends to Newton’s law; the tests of Secs. III, IV B, and IV D all lie there. Equation (16) holds in the solution of Einstein’s equations about the body, so where b<1b < 1b<1 Eq. (18) departs from them, as any account of flat rotation curves by the baryons alone must. The balance of Sec. III has every ring that a horizon gains take in one Landauer energy, which is the case b=1b = 1b=1. For b<1b < 1b<1 the field equations are not derived here, nor is the bending of light.

What reaches a string. The body’s energy per string of the sphere is E=Mc2/NsE = Mc^2/N_sE=Mc2/Ns​, the same for every string of the sphere. It is fixed by the body and the sphere alone, before the strings that carry the body’s information are picked out; those strings then hold the larger share E/bE/bE/b of Eq. (18). The cell and LLL enter only through their product, Lℓc=2πRΛL\lc = 2\pi\RLLℓc​=2πRΛ​. A string’s share of the body. A string that carries the body’s information is one of the body’s qubits (Postulate 1), part of the body itself. Mass is measured on the manifold, at places, and a place is a cell (Sec. II). The measurement finds the bits in those cells and nothing else (Postulate 1), so mass energy is counted in bits: cells without such bits show no mass. No cell differs from another (Postulate 2), so every bit counts the same. The strings hold the matter uuu per string, on the LLL bits of one whole qubit, so for f≤1f \le 1f≤1 a string’s share of the body, E=fuE = fuE=fu, fills the fraction fff of its bits, to within one bit. That fraction is the probability of Eq. (2), and its amplitude is f\sqrt ff​, Eq. (1). A share larger than uuu fills every bit, and the count ends there. We take its amplitude to keep growing as the square root of its energy, as a wave’s does: we use the same scale for every fff,

h=f=gN/a0.h = \sqrt f = \sqrt{g_N/a_0} .h=f​=gN​/a0​​.
(22)

On this scale h=1h = 1h=1 is one whole qubit. Near the body, where gN>a0g_N > a_0gN​>a0​, fff and hhh exceed one. The body’s share is then still held, since by Eq. (18) each string that carries the body’s information holds two Landauer energies at the sphere’s temperature, whatever fff is. So uuu sets the unit of hhh; it does not limit what a string holds.

Which strings carry the body’s information. A string either carries the body’s information or does not. A string that carries it takes its phase from the body’s state, as a laser locked to an injected signal takes its phase from the signal [86, 87]. The laser locks when the signal turns its phase, on each round trip, by more than the difference of the two frequencies makes it slip. For a string the round trip is one tick. A free tick turns the global phase of a string by Estc/ℏE_s\tc/\hbarEs​tc​/ℏ (Sec. II), with EsE_sEs​ the energy the string holds in the spread of Sec. IV E. Postulate 1 hides the value of the global phase, not its turn per tick, which defines the string’s energy. The body is at rest, so its share is the same at every tick, and the turn is the slip of the string’s global phase against the body’s. Treated as a point (above), the body is one cell, so in one tick its share reaches one cell of the string, which holds one of the string’s LLL bits: each tick brings 1/L1/L1/L of the share. As the injected signal adds to the laser’s field, these parts add as amplitudes: they arrive with the same phase at every tick, and a state is a linear combination of outcomes (Postulate 1). The share has the amplitude hhh against the string’s one whole qubit, and its LLL parts add up to it, so each tick adds the amplitude h/Lh/Lh/L. A state of unit amplitude that a tick turns by Δ\DeltaΔ, and to which the tick adds the smaller amplitude h/Lh/Lh/L at a fixed phase, has a phase that the tick leaves unchanged exactly when Δ\DeltaΔ is within arcsin⁡(h/L)\arcsin(h/L)arcsin(h/L) of a whole number of turns, as the Lean files prove. To leading order in 1/L1/L1/L the share can therefore turn the string’s global phase by at most h/Lh/Lh/L per tick. Where the slip per tick is larger, the global phase slips at every tick and the string takes no phase from the body. Where it is smaller, the ticks draw the global phase to a phase that they leave unchanged, as the Lean files also prove. The share is the same at every tick, and the law is that of the state that the ticks leave unchanged, in which the string holds that phase. A string therefore carries the body’s information when Estc/ℏ≤h/LE_s\tc/\hbar \le h/LEs​tc​/ℏ≤h/L, that is, when Es≤h kBTdSE_s \le h\,k_BT_{\rm dS}Es​≤hkB​TdS​, by Eq. (11). The strings’ energies are spread at the horizon’s temperature (Sec. IV E), by the principle of maximum entropy [88], so the fraction e−he^{-h}e−h of them lies above h kBTdSh\,k_BT_{\rm dS}hkB​TdS​, and those strings miss the body. The exceptions are the strings that a tick turns to within arcsin⁡(h/L)\arcsin(h/L)arcsin(h/L) of one or more whole turns. A whole turn is no turn, so they carry the body’s information too; they are a fraction below e−3πL/2e^{-3\pi L/2}e−3πL/2 of the strings. A string’s threshold on the scale of hhh is thus θ=Es/kBTdS\theta = E_s/k_BT_{\rm dS}θ=Es​/kB​TdS​, with mean one. The strings that carry the body’s information are therefore the fraction

b=1−e−h.b = 1 - e^{-h} .b=1−e−h.
(23)

The law. Equations (18), (22), and (23) give

a=gN1−e−gN/a0,a = \frac{g_N}{1 - e^{-\sqrt{g_N/a_0}}} ,a=1−e−gN​/a0​​gN​​,

with a0a_0a0​ from Eq. (21). This is the function that McGaugh, Lelli, and Schombert fitted to the radial acceleration relation, measured at 2693 points in 153 galaxies, with a0=(1.20±0.02±0.24)×10−10a_0 = (1.20\pm0.02\pm0.24)\times10^{-10}a0​=(1.20±0.02±0.24)×10−10 m s−2^{-2}−2, the second error systematic [28]. Desmond’s analysis, which fits each galaxy’s distance, inclination, and mass-to-light ratios along with the relation, gives (1.19±0.04±0.09)×10−10(1.19\pm0.04\pm0.09)\times10^{-10}(1.19±0.04±0.09)×10−10 m s−2^{-2}−2 [74]. A classical share. A string’s share of the body enters as an amplitude because a string that carries the body’s information is one of its qubits (Postulate 1). If the share were classical, a string would hold a record of the body with the probability fff. Then bbb would fall as fff far from the body, and aaa would tend to the constant a0a_0a0​, so rotation speeds would rise as r\sqrt rr​. Flat rotation curves therefore support Postulate 1.

The frame of the law. Equation (24) is derived on a sphere centered on all the mass inside it, at rest, with the same acceleration at every point of the sphere. That acceleration entered through its Unruh temperature, Eq. (16), and an Unruh temperature is that of a proper acceleration: the acceleration of an observer held at rest relative to the body, against local free fall. In the manifold a uniform external field, such as the Galaxy’s across the solar system, is a common acceleration of the body and of local free fall at the place of every such observer. So it changes no proper acceleration, and hence neither the sphere’s temperature nor the share. Equation (24) therefore holds in the body’s freely falling frame as for an isolated body, and of an external field only its tide, the variation across the sphere, enters. Here the law parts from the field equations of MOND, in which the external field enters the nonlinearity whole [90]; Sec. IV B gives the quadrupole that this difference decides. Two bodies of comparable mass have no sphere centered on all the mass at rest, since each falls in the other’s field, which is not uniform across a sphere about it; the law for such a pair is not derived here. For a test body in the field of a mass the law stands, with no external-field effect. Wide binary stars in the Galaxy’s field, of comparable masses, are where the Gaia data are read: one analysis finds an excess over Newton of 1.43±0.061.43\pm0.061.43±0.06 at gN=10−10.15g_N = 10^{-10.15}gN​=10−10.15 m s−2^{-2}−2 [91], another none [92]. A test body there would show 1.871.871.87, Eq. (24); the pair awaits the two-body law.

Why the temperature cannot lead. The floor Ec/L\Ec/LEc​/L could be taken as the mechanism instead of the strings. If gravity followed the excess of the combined temperature over the floor, as Milgrom proposed [72], Eq. (16) would give a=gN2+2aΛgNa = \sqrt{g_N^2 + 2a_\Lambda g_N}a=gN2​+2aΛ​gN​​. That has the deep form, but with the scale 2c2/RΛ2c^2/\RL2c2/RΛ​, nine times the observed a0a_0a0​, which rejects it; and its transition is 38% above Newton’s law at gN=10a0g_N = 10a_0gN​=10a0​, where the observed relation is 4% above. The floor thus marks the scale, but the coefficient comes from the strings’ energy.

This framework has no dark-matter halo, nor the smearing of energy-momentum over neighboring spacetimes by which Invariant Set Theory reaches the same phenomena with Λ=0\Lambda = 0Λ=0 [40, 75]. Galactic rotation is set by the baryons, GGG, and the horizon radius, which Λ\LambdaΛ fixes. The known difficulties of any such account, galaxy clusters [76] and the acoustic peaks of the microwave background [77], are not addressed here and remain open.

D. Cosmological scale: the ring

Einstein’s equations, Eq. (13), leave the value of Λ\LambdaΛ free. Consider a body of mass MMM at rest, alone, with M=0M = 0M=0 allowed. Times c4/Gc^4/Gc4/G, this is the first law of the horizon with Λ\LambdaΛ free, d(Mc2)=−T dS+V dPd(Mc^2) = -T\,dS + V\,dPd(Mc2)=−TdS+VdP, with V=4πrc3/3V = 4\pi r_c^3/3V=4πrc3​/3 and P=−Λc4/8πGP = -\Lambda c^4/8\pi GP=−Λc4/8πG [79]. The Clausius relation takes all the energy that crosses as heat, so the work V dPV\,dPVdP is zero, and dΛ=0d\Lambda = 0dΛ=0: Λ\LambdaΛ is the same at every mass, and we may find it in the solution without one.

Without a mass the laws and the state are the same at every place and in every direction (Sec. II). The geometry of space is a quantity, defined by qubits (Postulate 1), so the laws and the state alone set it: the space at an instant of an observer at rest has the same geometry at every place and in every direction, and so, by Schur’s lemma, one curvature, KKK [45]. It is totally geodesic, since the geometry about the observer does not change in time [44]. A largest ring can run through any place in any direction (Sec. II), and by Postulate 2 it is a closed geodesic of space, of length LℓcL\lcLℓc​. So every geodesic of this space closes, all after that one length, and the space is complete (Hopf–Rinow [45]). Space has three dimensions here, as observed; a companion preprint derives the number [35]. By the Killing–Hopf theorem [45] the space is then the three-sphere, Euclidean space, or hyperbolic space, divided by a group of isometries that acts freely and properly discontinuously. In Euclidean or hyperbolic space a geodesic closes only through the group, so the group would carry a point onto every point of a sphere about it, infinitely many in a bounded region, which such a group cannot do. The space is therefore a three-sphere divided by a finite group of rotations, with K>0K > 0K>0. Einstein’s constraint on this slice without matter gives 3K=Λ3K = \Lambda3K=Λ [42], so Λ>0\Lambda > 0Λ>0. The group is trivial. A rotation of the three-sphere other than ±1\pm1±1 turns some plane through the center by an angle θ\thetaθ with 0<θ<2π0 < \theta < 2\pi0<θ<2π. When the antipodal map is in the group too, θ≠π\theta \ne \piθ=π: otherwise the antipodal map composed with the rotation would fix that plane, and the group acts freely. So the largest ring in that plane closes after less than a full turn, and after less than half a turn when the antipodal map is in the group. Now take a unit vector eee and a plane QQQ orthogonal to it, and the planes spanned by eee and a unit vector of QQQ, a one-parameter family. A rotation of the group other than ±1\pm1±1 carries at most one of them onto itself. Carrying two, it would carry eee onto a multiple of itself, −e-e−e since it fixes nothing, and each of their two unit vectors of QQQ onto its negative; so it would be −1-1−1 on three dimensions and hence, fixing nothing, on all of space. A finite group therefore leaves some plane of the family, carried onto itself by no rotation of the group but ±1\pm1±1, and the largest ring in that plane closes only after a full turn, or half a turn when the antipodal map is in the group. The largest rings have one length, so the group holds at most the antipodal map. The rings through an observer’s cell exclude that map. They meet at his place and again at the opposite of his cell, half a ring’s length along each (Sec. II). With the antipodal points identified, the point halfway around a great circle is its starting point, so a ring’s LLL cells run along half a great circle, and the opposite cell, L/2L/2L/2 cells on, lies a quarter of a great circle from his place; two of the L/2L/2L/2 rings through his cell would then run along the one great circle through both places. The cells one step from his cell on these two rings would fall on the same places, and so would be the same cells (Sec. II). Yet these cells are neither his cell nor its opposite, and two rings through a cell share only that cell and its opposite. So the space at an instant is the three-sphere itself, and every largest ring, a great circle of it, has the length 2π3/Λ2\pi\sqrt{3/\Lambda}2π3/Λ​. Eq. (5) gives 3/Λ=RΛ\sqrt{3/\Lambda} = \RL3/Λ​=RΛ​, so Λ=3/RΛ2\Lambda = 3/\RL^2Λ=3/RΛ2​ with a mass and without, which fixes the integration constant.

In the solution without a mass, de Sitter space, an observer at rest has a cosmological horizon, the farthest he can ever see, of radius 3/Λ=RΛ\sqrt{3/\Lambda} = \RL3/Λ​=RΛ​ and at the proper distance πRΛ/2\pi\RL/2πRΛ​/2 from him, a quarter lap of a largest ring [39]. In the register his horizon lies L/4L/4L/4 steps from his cell, and every largest ring, through his cell or not, has half its cells inside it, counting a cell on it as half (Sec. IV C). That half carries the entropy inside his horizon; the horizon’s own entropy is the register’s count, Eq. (7). The manifold puts him at the center of a two-sphere of area 4πRΛ24\pi\RL^24πRΛ2​, each of its great circles a closed geodesic of a ring’s length. The manifold and the register are linked as in Sec. II: the largest rings are closed geodesics, along which the cells measure distance, here a quarter lap to the horizon, and the count, RRR strings with one bit each, gives each string its share of the area. Neither says where the rings that do not pass through his cell lie: the manifold describes the register’s incidence only for the rings through his cell (Sec. II). Two rings that do not pass through his cell also share a cell, by Postulate 2, but no step of the paper uses where that cell lies: the count of Eq. (8) uses only the number of rings and their lengths, and the share of Sec. IV C only distances along rings.

With Λ=3/RΛ2\Lambda = 3/\RL^2Λ=3/RΛ2​ and Eq. (14), Newton’s constant and the cosmological constant are not independent of each other,
